one_liner: Header-only C++20 work-stealing thread pool and task-graph runner, under 600 lines, benchmarked faster than Taskflow on fine-grained tasks.
what_it_does: Provides scheduling::ThreadPool with Submit(callable), Submit(Task*) and Submit(container of Task), plus Wait() and a Wait(predicate) overload that keeps executing queued tasks on the calling thread. Task graphs are built from a container of scheduling::Task objects linked with Succeed()/Precede(); tasks can be cancelled and reset, and a finished graph can be resubmitted. It is not API-compatible with Taskflow: there is no Executor/Taskflow object, no subflows, no parallel algorithms (for_each, reduce) and no futures or return values.
how_it_is_fast: One Chase-Lev work-stealing deque per worker (the lock-free deque copied from Google Filament, made growable with Taskflow's Array buffer) plus one extra queue for non-worker threads; the queue is chosen through a thread_local index instead of a thread-id map. When a task finishes, the first successor whose predecessor count hits zero runs inline on the same worker (continuation passing), so a linear chain never touches a queue. The recursive Fibonacci pattern uses Wait(predicate), which helps by running queued tasks instead of creating Taskflow-style subflow graphs, which is where most of the 9x gap comes from.
when_to_use: Many tiny fire-and-forget tasks or recursive fork-join code on a single pool, where per-task overhead dominates (recursive Fibonacci was about 9x faster than Taskflow 3.7 subflows at n=35 in the author's run).
Long dependency chains or sparse DAGs of small tasks, where inline execution of the ready successor avoids queue traffic (linear chain of 33.5M tasks: 4.16 s vs 9.95 s).
Projects that want a tiny, readable, vendorable scheduler (one header, no dependencies) and are on C++20.
Statically linked binaries on Linux, macOS or Windows (CI covers GCC 13, Clang, MSVC, with TSAN/ASAN/UBSAN jobs).
when_not_to_use: Data-parallel loops or coarse task graphs: the matrix-multiplication task graph was slower than Taskflow at every size (2048: 4,134 ms vs 3,970 ms; 256: 8.20 ms vs 4.13 ms), and there are no built-in parallel algorithms.
Shared libraries or plugins: the README states dynamic linking is unsupported because of the static thread_local queue index.

Several threads that are not pool workers submitting concurrently, or more than one ThreadPool in a process: all non-worker threads push into the same owner-only Chase-Lev deque (index 0), and the thread_local index is shared by every ThreadPool instance, so a worker of one pool submitting to another pool pushes into that pool's queue i (racing its owner, or out of range if the second pool is smaller). Neither case is documented as safe.
Power- or CPU-sensitive deployments: idle workers spin through 100 steal attempts before blocking, keep spinning while any task is outstanding, and Wait(predicate) is a pure busy loop.

Projects needing exceptions, priorities, futures or long-term maintenance: an exception escaping a task terminates the program (no handling in Execute), there are no releases, and the last commit is from November 2024.

integration.dependencies: none (Google Benchmark, Taskflow v3.7.0 and GoogleTest are fetched only for the benchmarks/tests)
integration.min_toolchain: C++20 (concepts, std::atomic wait/notify); CMake 3.21 for the bundled CMakeLists
integration.platforms: any platform with C++20 threads and atomic wait; CI on Ubuntu (GCC 13, Clang), macOS, Windows MSVC
integration.thread_safety: Submit from worker threads is the intended path; submitting the same graph from several threads at once is forbidden by the README; concurrent Submit from multiple non-worker threads is not documented and pushes into one single-owner deque

gotchas: Task objects in a graph must not move or be destroyed until the pool finishes them (reserve the vector first); README issue #33 reported its own graph example printing 0 for every result (closed Oct 2024) and #35 a dangling reference in an example.
Recursive Wait(predicate), as in the Fibonacci example, grows the stack with recursion depth; the README warns it can overflow.

Deque indices top_/bottom_ are std::atomic<int> while Array::Get/Put take size_t; top_ only ever increases, so a queue that sees more than about 2^31 steals in one pool lifetime overflows a signed int. Old buffers after a resize are kept until the pool is destroyed.

Benchmark harness asymmetries: Google Benchmark's CPU-time column counts only the main thread, so the CPU-time charts (e.g. matmul 11.9 ms vs 29.5 ms) say nothing about worker CPU use; the Taskflow matmul loop allocates the three n x n matrices inside the timed loop while the Scheduling loop allocates them once outside, which favours Scheduling yet it still loses; scripts/build.sh sets no CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE, and the README does not state the build type or flags used.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over nexus or ThunderBolt-HT when you need explicit dependency graphs with cancellation in one small, dependency-free C++20 header; pick Fork Union for parallel-for dispatch, and libfork, citor or Staccato when fork-join performance is the main goal and you want evidence measured against more than Taskflow.
verified_claims_summary: The author's Google Benchmark run (Scheduling commit ae8a367 vs Taskflow, built from benchmarks/taskflow.cmake at v3.7.0; compiler and flags not stated; hardware reported inconsistently as an 'Intel Xeon i7-1165G7' with 32 CPUs on Debian 12) shows wall time of 1,661 ms vs 15,058 ms for recursive Fibonacci(35) and 4,158 ms vs 9,951 ms for a 33,554,432-task linear chain, but Scheduling was slower on the matrix-multiplication task graph at every size; large sizes were single-iteration runs.
status_note: Stale (last commit November 2024, 37 commits, no releases, issue #38 about tasks_count_ accounting unanswered since November 2025), but MIT-licensed with Apache-2.0 Filament code and small enough to vendor and audit.
